dira may read session start, stop and working directory from the agent harness to
derive attention drift.

## What the founder chose, and against what advice

The recommendation in `qst-0002` — and mine — was **not to build this**. It is the
one proposed feature closer to self-surveillance than to navigation, and it is easy
to add and impossible to un-ship. That argument was made and did not win. It is
recorded here rather than dropped, because the next session should not re-litigate
it and should know it was a considered choice, not an oversight.

## The constraints this makes load-bearing

Two existing rules stop being background and become the implementation contract:

- **`cst-0004`, no network.** Where your time went never leaves the machine. There is
  no telemetry, no upload, no "anonymised" aggregate. A drift report is computed at
  read time from local files and printed.
- **`cst-0003`, private stays private.** Session metadata is private context by
  default and inherits every rule that already governs a private ledger: never
  exported downward, cited ref-only across a boundary, never rendered into a public
  surface. A public ledger renderer must not be able to say what a person was doing
  on Tuesday, and that has to be structural rather than a display choice.

## What must be true before it ships

**Reading is opt-in and off by default.** A tool that starts logging behaviour the
moment it is installed has made the choice for the user. The person who benefits
must have turned it on.

**The raw record is not kept.** What is stored is the derived answer — which ledgers
the week's sessions touched — not a timeline that could reconstruct a working day.
The difference between "70% of sessions were in repos unconnected to your focus" and
a per-session log is the whole distance between navigation and surveillance, and the
first can be computed without retaining the second.

**It is deletable in one command, and the command is documented next to the feature.**
